mcqs.question: Why do real recommendation systems typically merge candidates from several sources (two-tower collaborative, content-based, popularity) rather than relying on one candidate-generation method?
options: Because each source covers a different gap — collaborative signal is strong for established items and users, content-based covers thin-data new items, and popularity covers cold-start users — and no single source covers all three well
Because a single candidate source is always too slow to run at request time
Because regulations require at least three independent recommendation sources
Because merging sources eliminates the need for a separate ranking stage afterward
mcqs.explanation: Merging sources is about coverage, not speed — each method has a structural blind spot (new items, new users, or reliance on volume) that a different source fills. There's no such regulatory requirement, and merged candidates still need a ranking stage to determine final order.

mcqs.question: Why is launching a new recommender without a holdout/guardrail group risky, even if it performed well offline?
options: Because holdout groups are only necessary for fraud detection systems, not recommenders
Because without a holdout there's no way to compare against what would have happened under the old system, so a slow regression on a guardrail metric can go completely undetected
Because a holdout group is required to compute offline NDCG
Because launching without a holdout makes the model impossible to roll back later
mcqs.explanation: The risk is purely about detectability — a holdout is the only way to know what the counterfactual would have been, so a regression with no holdout can go unnoticed until it's already caused damage. Holdouts aren't specific to fraud systems, they're unrelated to computing offline NDCG, and rollback capability doesn't depend on having one.
